In machine learning, these concepts are critical for understanding loss functions, feature selection, regularization, and generative modeling."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Entropy: Measuring Uncertainty"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Entropy measures the expected amount of uncertainty or 'surprise' in a random variable. For a discrete probability distribution P(X), the Shannon entropy H(X) is defined as the sum over all possible outcomes."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import numpy as np

def calculate_entropy(prob_dist):
    # Avoid log(0) by filtering out zero probabilities
    prob_dist = np.array(prob_dist)
    prob_dist = prob_dist[prob_dist > 0]
    return -np.sum(prob_dist * np.log2(prob_dist))

# Example: Fair coin vs Biased coin
fair_coin = [0.5, 0.5]
biased_coin = [0.9, 0.1]
print(f"Entropy of fair coin: {calculate_entropy(fair_coin)}")
print(f"Entropy of biased coin: {calculate_entropy(biased_coin)}")"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"KL divergence measures how one probability distribution P diverges from a second, expected probability distribution Q. In machine learning, we often minimize KL divergence when training models to approximate an empirical data distribution."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"def kl_divergence(p, q):
    p = np.array(p)
    q = np.array(q)
    # Filter to avoid division by zero or log(0)
    mask = (p > 0) & (q > 0)
    return np.sum(p[mask] * np.log(p[mask] / q[mask]))

p = [0.4, 0.6]
q = [0.5, 0.5]
print(f"KL Divergence D(P || Q): {kl_divergence(p, q)}")"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Cross-Entropy Loss"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Cross-entropy builds directly on entropy and KL divergence. It measures the total number of bits required to events from one distribution when using the optimal code for another distribution. It is the standard loss function for multi-class classification."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Binary Cross-Entropy: Used for binary classification tasks, quantifying the difference between two probability distributions."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Categorical Cross-Entropy: Extends binary cross-entropy to N classes, heavily used alongside Softmax activation functions."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Defining predicted logits and true labels
logits = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, 0.1]])
targets = torch.tensor([0])

loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
loss = loss_fn(logits, targets)
print(f"PyTorch Cross-Entropy Loss: {loss.item()}")"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Mutual Information"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mutual Information (MI) measures the amount of information that one random variable contains about another. It is a powerful metric for non-linear feature selection because, unlike correlation, MI captures any kind of relationship between variables."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"If X and Y are completely independent, their Mutual Information is zero."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Higher mutual information indicates high reduction in uncertainty of one variable given the other."},{"order":18,"type":"heading","text":"Summary"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mastering information theory equips machine learning practitioners with the mathematical intuition needed to design better architectures, choose optimal loss functions, and evaluate data pipelines efficiently."}]
